summary.text: A nonzero determinant forces the matrix to contain a nonzero entry, so for some indices \(i,j\), both \(n+i-j\) and \(n+j-i\) are prime and their sum is \(2n\); taking \(n=2k+1\) gives the required decomposition for \(k\ge 60\). The remaining cases \(1\le k<60\) are handled by an explicit finite list of prime decompositions.

full_proof.text:
Let \(a(n)=A228623(n)\). For each positive integer \(n\), define the \(n\times n\) integer matrix \(M_n\), whose rows and columns are indexed by \(i,j\in\{0,1,\ldots,n-1\}\), by
\[
(M_n)_{ij}=
\begin{cases}
1,&\text{if both }n+i-j\text{ and }n+j-i\text{ are prime},\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
Here the expressions agree with the natural-number subtractions in the definition of the sequence. Indeed, because \(i,j<n\), we have
\[
j<n\le n+i\qquad\text{and}\qquad i<n\le n+j.
\]
Thus neither subtraction is truncated. By definition,
\[
a(n)=\det(M_n).
\]

We first establish the key consequence of a nonzero value of the sequence.

**Lemma.** If \(n>0\) and \(a(n)\ne0\), then there are primes \(p,q\) such that
\[
p+q=2n.
\]

**Proof of the lemma.** Since \(a(n)=\det(M_n)\ne0\), the matrix \(M_n\) cannot be the zero matrix: because \(n>0\), the determinant of the \(n\times n\) zero matrix is zero. Hence at least one entry \((M_n)_{ij}\) is nonzero. Every entry of \(M_n\) is either zero or one, so this entry must equal one. By the definition of the entries, the two natural numbers
\[
p=n+i-j,\qquad q=n+j-i
\]
are therefore both prime.

As noted above, the bounds \(0\le i,j<n\) imply \(n+i\ge j\) and \(n+j\ge i\), so these subtractions are ordinary exact subtractions. Consequently,
\[
p+q=(n+i-j)+(n+j-i)=2n.
\]
This proves the lemma.

Now assume the conjectured nonvanishing statement:
\[
\text{for every odd integer }n>120,\qquad a(n)\ne0.
\]
We prove that for every positive integer \(k\), the integer \(4k+2\) is a sum of two primes.

There are two cases.

### Case 1: \(1\le k<60\)

These finitely many cases are supplied by the following table. In every row the displayed numbers \(p,q\) are prime and satisfy \(p+q=4k+2\).

\[
\begin{array}{c|r@{\;}r||c|r@{\;}r||c|r@{\;}r}
k&p&q&k&p&q&k&p&q\\ \hline
1&3&3&21&3&83&41&3&163\\
2&3&7&22&7&83&42&3&167\\
3&3&11&23&5&89&43&7&167\\
4&5&13&24&19&79&44&5&173\\
5&3&19&25&5&97&45&3&179\\
6&3&23&26&3&103&46&5&181\\
7&7&23&27&3&107&47&11&179\\
8&3&31&28&5&109&48&3&191\\
9&7&31&29&5&113&49&5&193\\
10&5&37&30&13&109&50&3&199\\
11&3&43&31&13&113&51&7&199\\
12&3&47&32&3&127&52&11&199\\
13&7&47&33&3&131&53&3&211\\
14&5&53&34&7&131&54&7&211\\
15&3&59&35&3&139&55&11&211\\
16&5&61&36&7&139&56&3&223\\
17&3&67&37&11&139&57&3&227\\
18&3&71&38&3&151&58&5&229\\
19&5&73&39&7&151&59&5&233\\
20&3&79&40&5&157&&&
\end{array}
\]

The sum assertion in each row is immediate arithmetic. For completeness, the primality assertions are also a finite elementary check. Every number displayed is at most \(233<17^2\). The numbers \(3,5,7,11,13\) are prime directly, and each displayed number greater than \(13\) is not divisible by any of
\[
2,3,5,7,11,13.
\]
If such a number were composite, it would have a prime divisor no larger than its square root, hence a prime divisor less than \(17\), necessarily one from that list. The indicated divisibility checks therefore establish the primality of every entry in the table. Thus the desired Goldbach representation holds for every \(k\) in this first case.

### Case 2: \(k\ge60\)

Set
\[
n=2k+1.
\]
Then \(n\) is odd. Moreover,
\[
n=2k+1\ge2\cdot60+1=121>120.
\]
The assumed conjecture therefore gives
\[
a(n)\ne0.
\]
Also \(n>0\), so the lemma applies. We obtain primes \(p,q\) satisfying
\[
p+q=2n.
\]
Substituting \(n=2k+1\) yields
\[
p+q=2(2k+1)=4k+2.
\]
Thus \(4k+2\) is a sum of two primes in the second case as well.

The two cases cover every positive integer \(k\). Therefore, if \(a(n)\ne0\) for every odd \(n>120\), then every integer of the form \(4k+2\) with \(k>0\) is the sum of two primes.
